provenance.layout: drawing - Figure 1-12 of the Casa C100G Hardware Installation Guide (rev 07/08/2022), "RF IO upstream and downstream modules", which draws all three rear I/O cards side by side. Port COUNT, port ORDER and the column arrangement are read straight off it and are reliable; positions are taken as fractions of the drawn plate, measured by colour detection at 600 dpi
provenance.mcx-is-recessed: THE OWNER, AGAINST THE HARDWARE: "the MCX connector is RECESSED INTO the faceplate, so it actually doesn't stick out from the faceplate, it's recessed from the faceplate ... whereas the US I/O and the DS I/Os have the F fitting STICKING OUT of the faceplate." So the two connector families on these chassis go OPPOSITE WAYS - MCX recessed, F-type proud - and that is a fact about the world, recorded in his terms so it does not have to be rediscovered. THIS SENTENCE IS COPIED FROM casa/io-6p12-sw@2, where it was written first. One statement from one person about one pair of connector families, restated on every card it applies to - not several observations that agreed. THE FIGURES AGREE, INDEPENDENTLY AND AFTERWARDS. Figure 1-12 (C100G), "RF IO upstream and downstream modules", draws the three rear I/O cards side by side and treats the families completely differently: every F port on QAM IO and US IO is a HEX NUT with concentric rings and a shadow, a connector body standing off the plate, while every MCX port on UPS IO 32 is a small flat dark circle with no hex and no body. Figures 1-15 and 1-16 draw the 6+12 cards' MCX the same flat way. NOTHING IS CHANGED HERE YET, and the reason is not indecision. The aperture is composed from std/mcx@1, whose relief is {node: barrel, cyl: 2.0} - a PROTRUSION read off the Radiall R113.553.000 side elevation, which is a FRONT-MOUNT bulkhead jack whose flange does sit on the front of its panel. std/mcx@1 is not wrong about that connector; it is the wrong VARIANT for every card that composes it, and all five of its users are Casa. It is a std/ part and the registry note in spec/schemas/standards.yaml says the same thing, so the two have to move together and the decision is not this contract's to take. Reported to the team lead. NO DEPTH IS GUESSED: the owner gave a topology, not a dimension, and no Casa document gives a recess depth. WANTED: how far below the faceplate the MCX interface sits - one caliper reading or one side-on photograph.
provenance.missing-component: THE CABLE RETENTION PLATE IS A REAL PART AND THIS LIBRARY DOES NOT HAVE ONE. Figure 2-15 names it - "UPS 32x4 I/O cable retention plate" - and draws it as its own object: a notched strip with the port numbers printed between the notches and three screws through it. Figures 1-15 and 1-16 of the C100G guide draw the equivalent beside the 6+12 and 6+12 SW I/O cards, captioned "w/ cable retention bracket". The three standoffs on this card exist for no other purpose than to carry it. So this is a MISSING COMPONENT, not a missing decision: casa/ has no cable-retention-plate and none of the four I/O card families can seat one. It is recorded rather than built because building it is a modelling job with its own sourcing, not part of a relief pass. Note it is NOT casa/cable-manager, which is a different part on the chassis front. `rf-field` stays a silkscreen outline and is now CONFIRMED as one: Figure 2-15 makes it unambiguous that the rectangle is where that plate seats.
provenance.numbering: drawing - the RIGHT column is even (0, 2 ... 30) and the LEFT column odd (1, 3 ... 31), with both numbers printed BELOW their row. Read at 4x from the 600 dpi render; at page scale the pair reads as one number
provenance.photograph: CONFIRMED against the real card - the "32 port" photograph on the Casa US16x8 datasheet (2018). Sixteen rows of two, both numbers printed BELOW their row with the right column even and the left odd, "UPS IO 32" under a SINGLE orange band, and the three captive screws at the row-pair mid-points. The shot is taken at an angle, so it settles what is there and not where anything is; the one thing it settles that the figure got wrong is the shape of the screw heads
provenance.ports: drawing - Table A-9 of the same guide, headed "RFU specifications", gives "32 ports x 4 channels per port using UPS 32x4 I/O module" and a connector row reading, for that module, "MCX (micro coaxial), 50 ohm, European CECC 22220". Casa naming CECC 22220 is the same specification the registry's `mcx` key cites, so the aperture composed here is the one Casa points at. Note the impedance - this card is 50-ohm MCX where the BDM's 6+12 I/O is 75-ohm MCX (Table A-10) - one mechanical interface, two impedances, which is why the panel hole is shared and the media attr is not
provenance.positions: drawing - two columns at 0.183 and 0.645 of the plate width, sixteen rows on a uniform 17.69 mm pitch from 43.29. The drawn row spacing varies from 16.0 to 19.8 mm, so a uniform pitch is fitted rather than each gap copied. The column pair's midline sits 2.6 mm left of the plate centre, which is where casa/io-6p12's two columns sit too (12.42 against 12.61) - two cards measured off two different figures agreeing to 0.2 mm is what makes the offset real rather than jitter
provenance.power: NO FIGURE. Table A-9 gives ports and connector only. Table A-4 gives the row "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" as 220 W for the US16x8 - that is the PAIR's figure and casa/us-16x8 already carries it with `power-draw-scope` of module-with-paired-io. Deriving this card's share by subtracting the 200 W RFU figure from the 220 W UPS 32x4 figure would be OUR arithmetic, not Casa's, and would also be wrong - the two numbers differ by the whole pairing, not by one card. L27 stands
provenance.relief: the C100G/C40G card family treatment - two captive screws (cyl 1.6), the ejector latch strip (out 4.2). THE FULL ARGUMENT IS IN casa/bdm@1 AND THIS IS A POINTER TO IT, not a second reading: the magnitudes are one estimate per kind of hardware, taken from edgecore/agr-panel-screw@1 for a screw head and edgecore/agr-psu-dc@1 for the ejector latch, applied across the family because these cards share a faceplate. No Casa document states a depth for any of them. Eleven cards carrying 4.2 is ONE estimate written eleven times, not eleven readings that agreed. NOTE this card has NO LAMPS, so the family's dome figure is deliberately not cited here - citing a source for a number a file does not carry is how an inert wrong claim gets started. The three round thumb screws take the same cyl 1.6; `rf-field` is still NOT relief, for the reason its own entry gives.
provenance.rf-field: drawing - the figure outlines the port field with a light rectangle, which is the footprint the cable retention plate seats against. Drawn as a silkscreen outline, not as relief, because nothing states its depth
provenance.size: ESTIMATED, and shared with the whole C100G/C40G rear-slot family. Figure 1-12 is schematic - it draws these three cards 309, 295 and 288 px wide for one physical card, and the guide's chassis aspect is 0.936 against a specified 0.844 - so nothing absolute is taken from it. The envelope is the rear-slot bay in the C100G device manifest, 30.47 x 345.5, and the depth is the family estimate carried by casa/io-6p12
provenance.standoffs-not-screws: THE RECORDED DRAWING-VERSUS-PHOTOGRAPH DISAGREEMENT ABOVE IS NOT A DISAGREEMENT. The `thumbscrews` entry has Figure 1-12 drawing three HEXAGONS and the US16x8 datasheet photograph showing three ROUND SLOTTED HEADS at the same three places, and resolves it by letting the photograph win. Figure 2-15 shows both at once and they are TWO DIFFERENT OBJECTS. That figure draws three things stacked and labels them: the "UPS 16x8 line card", the "UPS 32x4 I/O cable retention plate" and the "UPS 32x4 I/O module". The MODULE carries three HEX heads inside the outlined port field. The RETENTION PLATE, drawn separately above it, carries three ROUND SLOTTED SCREW HEADS at matching heights. So the hexagons are threaded STANDOFFS on the card and the round heads are the screws that fasten the plate to them - and the datasheet photograph was taken WITH THE PLATE FITTED, which is why it shows round heads where the figure shows hex. Both sources were right about different objects. This is the trap the modelling notes name in as many words: before recording a source disagreement, check that both sources are talking about the same thing. WHAT CHANGES: the three nodes are standoffs, so cyl 1.6 - a panel screw HEAD height - was the wrong kind of number for them, not merely the wrong value. They now carry 9.5. WHERE THE 9.5 COMES FROM, AND WHAT IT IS NOT: it is the 3/8in Jason read off the C40G rear photograph for the 6+12 I/O cards standoffs, recorded in casa/io-6p12@2. It is adopted here because Figure 2-15 shows the same kind of hex standoff carrying the same kind of retention plate on this card. THAT IS ONE READING APPLIED TO A SECOND PART, NOT A SECOND READING - the two cards agreeing about it would be an echo, and if their standoffs differ this is the first assumption to break. No figure or table gives this card its own standoff height. WANTED: a caliper, or a side-on photograph of a UPS 32x4 with the plate off.
provenance.thumbscrews: drawing AND photograph, which disagree, and the photograph wins. Figure 1-12 puts three captive thumb screws on the column midline at the mid-point of the row pairs (0,1), (14,15) and (28,29), and draws them as HEXAGONS; the product photograph on the Casa US16x8 datasheet, captioned "32 port", shows the same three at the same three places with ROUND slotted heads, noticeably larger than an MCX jack. They are drawn round here. The installation procedure names them - "attach the UPS 32x4 cable retention plate using the three captive thumb screws at the front of the plate". How far they stand proud is NOT stated and is not modelled - casa/io-6p12's brass standoffs were measured at 9.5 mm on a photograph, but that is a different card and copying the number would be inventing one

components.description: Casa US 16X4 upstream line card for the C100G/C40G CCAP chassis. DOCSIS Control & Upstream module (DCU). Sixteen upstream burst receivers, but the RF connectors are on the paired rear RF Upstream I/O (RFU) module - this faceplate carries no connectors at all, only the STATUS, ALARM and ACTIVE lamps.
components.name: us-16x4

provenance.cutouts: NONE - this card has no aperture of any kind, which is the whole point of the split. The eight QAM or sixteen burst-receiver ports belong to the rear RFD/RFU I/O module, and Tables A-8 and A-9 of the install guide give those their F-type and MCX connectors
provenance.depth-known-wrong: THE 380.0 IS NOT MERELY UNMEASURED, IT IS IMPOSSIBLE, and this contract now says so in a field a tool can read - size-confidence: {d: known-wrong}. THE CONSTRAINT. Front and rear cards MEET AT A MIDPLANE, which the owner photographed: working/photos/casa/c40g-empty-midplane.png shows the emptied cage with the card guides and the midplane at the back of it, and the opening where the rear I/O card reaches through to the front card. So a front card and its rear partner have to share the chassis depth - 386.0 on the C100G, 388.45 on the C40G. Two cards at 380.0 need 760, which is not a wide error bar, it is twice the box. WHAT THE SHAPE IS, from the owner: "the front card is mostly rectangular, but the I/O card is kind of L SHAPED where the top part of the top connector PASSES THROUGH THE MIDPLANE and plugs into the front card, and the other one is plugged into the midplane. So they ultimately kind of meet in the middle." So the rear card is a body against the midplane PLUS A TONGUE at the top reaching forward through it. NOTE WHAT THAT DOES AND DOES NOT ALLOW, because the obvious rule is wrong. front + rear CAN exceed the chassis depth, by about the tongue length, because the tongue overlaps the front card at a height where the front card is not - they interleave rather than tile. The constraint is therefore an inequality with slack, not an equality. What it cannot absorb is a 374 mm overlap where a tongue is tens of millimetres. ONE PHOTOGRAPH IS USABLE AND IT IS NOT THIS CARD-FAMILY-WIDE. bdm2m-solder-side.jpeg has the faceplate FULLY IN FRAME, so its 345.5 long axis anchors the scale at 5.00 px/mm; the card measures 1336 px from the faceplate to the top of its midplane connectors. Raw that is 267 mm. The shot is NOT orthographic - the PCB reads 4.66 percent wider at the connector end than at the faceplate end, which is perspective, not a taper - so correcting to the mean scale gives about 261, and taking the card top at the outermost connector edge instead pushes it to about 282. CALL IT 270 PLUS OR MINUS 12 AND DO NOT ROUND THAT AWAY. REJECTED, and the rejection is the useful part: bdm2m-top-plan.jpeg and both qam-io-card plan shots have the faceplate CLIPPED BY THE FRAME, so the 345.5 anchor is truncated and every number off them is understated by an unknown amount. Measured anyway, the top-plan gives 227 mm for the same card the solder side gives 270 - a 19 percent disagreement that is entirely the broken anchor. They are not second opinions and must not be averaged in. NOTHING IS REPLACED. 270 plus or minus 12 is one reading of one card from one photograph that fails gate 1, and stamping it on twelve cards would be the family-number pattern doing harm instead of good - these cards share a FACEPLATE, which is established, not a depth, which is not. What is established is that 380.0 cannot be true. WANTED, in order of how much each unlocks: a tape on any one front card (fixes it outright); a tape on any one rear I/O card; an unclipped side-on photograph of a rear card showing where the tongue begins, which would give the midplane position and both halves at once.
provenance.faceplate-hardware-photo: THE OWNER SUPPLIED AN ISOMETRIC OF THE C100G FRONT and it corrects the SHAPE of two things on this faceplate. working/photos/casa/ - c100g-front-isometric.png and the crop crop-ejectors.png, read at high zoom. WHAT IT SETTLES: - The captive screw is not a flat slotted head. It is a substantial BLACK KNURLED KNOB standing well proud, with a dark top face and a light metallic band. `knurl` is added for that reason - it is a shape fact and costs no dimension. The drawn 2D head is still a slotted circle and is NOT redrawn; the figures draw it that way and this photograph cannot give a true elevation of it. - The EJECTOR LEVER is the most prominent thing on the whole face: a large CURVED BLACK lever, not the rounded strip this skin draws, with a thin vertical linkage rod running down the card from the knob to it. - RELATIVE PROMINENCE, which is the one quantitative thing a perspective view CAN give: lever stands proud of knob stands proud of lamp. This contract already orders them that way - 4.2, 1.6, 0.3 - so the photograph CONFIRMS the ordering rather than correcting it. Only the absolute magnitudes are understated, and it gives no absolute magnitude. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and why nothing else moved. It is a three-quarter view: every forward projection is foreshortened by an unknown factor, nothing of known size is in frame, and the one feature that looks measurable - the knob ellipse - needs a diameter nobody has. So it fails gate 1 outright, exactly as the Cisco perspective figures did. THE LEVER SILHOUETTE IS DELIBERATELY NOT REDRAWN: the true elevation outline of a curved lever is precisely what a three-quarter crop cannot give, and drawing sixteen faceplates from it would replace a sourced schematic strip with an invented curve. The 4.2 stays, marked `borrowed`. WANTED, and it closes both at once: ONE STRAIGHT-ON PHOTOGRAPH OF A SINGLE CARD, with a rule or any part of known size in frame. That would give the lever its silhouette AND its projection, and it is the cheapest open question on this family. THIS ENTRY IS ONE READING OF ONE PHOTOGRAPH restated across the thirteen front-slot cards that share this faceplate. The photograph shows DS 8X96, US 16X4 and SMM 8X10G specifically; the rest inherit it because the family shares a plate, which the DS/US positions provenance already establishes to the millimetre. It is NOT thirteen observations. The REAR cards - the 6+12 I/O family, rfd, rfu-16x8, ups-32x4, lc-sw-bdm and the two SMM Switch BDMs - are NOT in this photograph and are deliberately left alone.
provenance.layout: drawing - Figure 1-11 of the Casa C100G Hardware Installation Guide (rev 07/08/2022) draws US 16X4, US 16X8, DS 8X8, DS 8X96 and DS 8X192 side by side on ONE shell. It is authoritative for WHAT is on the face - which is nothing but three lamps, because the RF connectors live on the rear I/O module - and for the lamp ORDER, which is STATUS, ALARM, ACTIVE and is NOT the STATUS, ACTIVE, ALARM order the SMM and CSC faceplates use
provenance.leds: drawing-measured - Figure 1-17 of the C40G Hardware Installation Guide (rev 07/07/2022), "DOCSIS downstream and upstream line cards", which draws US 16X4, US 16X8, DS 8X8, DS 8X96 and DS 8X192 side by side. THIS CARD'S OWN PLATE was boxed at 108 x 1407 px, un- clipped, with clear white margin above and below, and its three lamp centres read at 0.57036, 0.58102, 0.59133 of that height. The figure's own spacing wobbles by half a pixel, so the pitch is the group's span divided evenly: 0.010483 of the height. Anchored to the 345.5 height this contract already holds, that is a pitch of 3.62 mm and centres at 197.06, 200.68 and 204.30. THE OTHER FOUR PLATES IN THE SAME FIGURE WERE MEASURED SEPARATELY AND AGREE TO WITHIN A PIXEL, which is said here rather than left for silence to imply; they are five instances of one drawing, not five sources. The order is STATUS, ALARM, ACTIVE with the dark lamp in the MIDDLE, which the figure shows by colour as well as by label - unlike the SMM pair, where ALARM is third and dark. It replaces a 6.6 mm pitch that was never measured on this card or on any other: casa/bdm's provenance said outright that 6.6 was picked so the lamps would "read as separate indicators", and the same three numbers had been carried onto every Casa front card. This entry is a separate reading of a separate plate and is not that number under a new name. THE 3.0 LAMP DIAMETER IS UNCHANGED AND STILL UNMEASURED, for the reason the BDM gave: these drawings are anisotropic, so a round lamp scales to two different diameters depending on the axis, which tells you the drawing is wrong rather than telling you the size.
provenance.positions: drawing, reconciled against casa/bdm - these are the BDM's numbers to the millimetre, because the BDM and the DQM/DCU cards are ONE faceplate. Figure 1-14 (the BDM) and Figure 1-11 (the DQM/DCU) put the bands, both stripe groups and the lamp cluster within 0.5mm of each other, and casa/bdm was built from the first of them. The DS8x96 photograph, scaled by the full card height, puts the stripe groups 5.6 and 8.0mm lower; that is a three-quarter view's perspective error over a 345.5mm card rather than a real difference, and six of these cards sit side by side in a C100G where a 6mm offset between two members of one family would read as a modelling fault. The lamp pitch is the one place the figure is the outlier: it draws the dots nearly touching on a 3.6 pitch, the photograph measures 8.14, and casa/bdm's 6.6 is carried
provenance.positions-rejected: photo-measured - taken as FRACTIONS of the known 345.5 card height from the DS8x96 data sheet product photograph. Figure 1-11 fails the orthographic gate: its plate renders 147 x 1951 px, aspect 0.0753 against the real 0.0882, so it is drawn about 15 percent narrow, and its five cards are drawn small enough that the lamp dots are squeezed onto a 3.6 pitch. Scaled by the full card height the photograph puts them on 8.14, and the DS8x96 and SMM300G photographs independently agree with each other on the two legend bands to within 0.5mm. So the photograph is used for placement and the figure for arrangement
provenance.power-draw-max-w: install guide - Table A-4 of the C100G install guide: 'Power consumption: Single DCU w/ RFU I/O - US16x4: 150W'. This card is end-of-life and has no findable data sheet, so the install guide is the only source - but it IS a source. The figure is transcribed, not estimated, and it is 50 W below the US16x8 sibling it was assumed to match
provenance.power-scope: READ THIS BEFORE SUMMING. Casa does not state a bare card's draw. Every figure in Tables A-3 and A-4 is the card PLUS its paired rear RF I/O module - the vendor's own column headings are 'Maximum consumption with I/O module', 'Single QAM w/ QAM I/O' and 'Single DCU w/ RFU I/O'. On a C100G that pairing spans TWO bays, a front DOCSIS card and a rear RF I/O card, so power-draw-max-w here already accounts for both and adding a rear I/O figure to it would double count. That the pairing is what is measured is not an inference: the same US16x8 is 200W with the F-connector RFU and 220W with the UPS 32x4 MCX I/O, which is one card and two answers. A single per-card key may be the wrong shape for these devices; that is a schema question, and until it is settled this note is what stops the number being read as something the vendor never said
provenance.relief: the C100G/C40G card family treatment - two captive screws (cyl 1.6), the ejector latch strip (out 4.2) and the 3 status lamps (dome 0.3). THE FULL ARGUMENT IS IN casa/bdm@1 AND THIS IS A POINTER TO IT, not a second reading: the three magnitudes are one estimate per kind of hardware, taken from edgecore/agr-panel-screw@1, edgecore/agr-psu-dc@1 and common/led-dot@1 - NONE of which measured them, which is why all three are tokened `estimated` rather than `borrowed` - applied across the family because these cards share a faceplate. No Casa document states a depth for any of them. Eleven cards carrying 4.2 is ONE estimate written eleven times, not eleven readings that agreed.

components.description: Cisco ASR 9900 Series 4T Service Edge Line Card, 5th generation. Ten QSFP-DD ports, each capable of 10, 40, 100, 200 or 400 Gigabit Ethernet, for 4 Tbps of aggregate bandwidth.
components.name: a99-10x400ge-x-se

provenance.cages: composed from std/, not drawn. Ganged QSFP pitch measures 18.73 mm off the art against the registry's TE-measured 19.0, so Cisco's shared-wall block is about 1.4 percent tighter; the measured PITCH is carried and the registry's APERTURE is carried, which leaves a nominal 0.23 mm wall. Aperture size is a governed dimension and a drawing is not the place to take it from.
provenance.frame: the card is modelled PORTRAIT - x across the card's thickness, y along its width - which is the stencil's own frame and casa's. WHICH WAY A CHASSIS CARRIES IT is the Overview and Reference Guide's 'Chassis Slots' section, quoted because an earlier version of this note had it wrong for three chassis out of seven: 'Cisco ASR 9010 Router: All line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted VERTICALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card. Cisco ASR 9006 Router and Cisco ASR 9904 Router: All chassis line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted HORIZONTALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card. Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' So only the ASR 9006 and the ASR 9904 lay their cards flat and rotate the bay; the other five place this component unrotated. The ejector-lever wording is the tell and it is why the guide is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing - 'top and bottom' means vertical, 'left and right ends' means horizontal, and the RU height of a chassis does not decide it.
provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. CAUTION for anyone re-deriving this: index.json's props.height_in and width_in are the Visio SHAPE box, not the card. They read 1.72 x 14.75 in for EVERY card master, against the datasheet's 1.63 x 15.58 in, and are 5 percent out in both axes. The ART is orthographic and does carry geometry: taking Cisco's stated W - which the spec table says 'includes ejector bracket/lever' - as the full long extent of the art puts the faceplate rectangle at 41.6 mm against a stated H of 41.4, inside half a percent, which is the gate-1 check. So the drawing is the ruler and the shape box is not.
provenance.leds: install guide - 'Each line card has a single tristate Status LED to display card status. Each ... port on the line card has a port status LED visible on the front panel.' The state vocabulary on both is Table 32, 'Port Status and Line Card Status LEDs', of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, transcribed rather than summarised: the card lamp's amber is TWO states, steady during boot and blinking for a software configuration error.
provenance.lifecycle: searched - no end-of-life notice for this part number is in the intake.
provenance.not-drawn: one thing on the real faceplate is deliberately NOT modelled: the coloured outlines that box each port group. They are real printing - the install guide spells the scheme out for the 400G combo card, 'Ports 0-5 (blue), 10-15 (red), 20-25 (magenta), 30-35 (orange)' - and the stencil draws them per group in solid and dashed strokes. They are omitted because the stencil builds them from many short stroked segments rather than closed rectangles, and guessing at a box that reads as a group boundary would put a line on the drawing that no measurement supports. Port grouping is carried structurally instead, by the port ids and by the lamp clusters that sit at each group's end.
provenance.ports: install guide - '10-Port 400-Gigabit Ethernet Line Cards with QSFPDD ... provides ten ports for QSFPDD modules that are capable of 10Gb, 40Gb, 100Gb, 200Gb, and 400Gb Ethernet traffic support', Figure 23 callout 2.
provenance.power: NOT STATED, and this is the record of it. The per-card power table for this family is Table 35, 'Ethernet Line Card Power Consumption Values', in the Cisco ASR 9000 Series Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, and it is the only per-card power table in the 78-document intake - the Overview and Reference Guide's Table 23 covers RSP, RP and fabric cards only and refers line cards to it. Table 35 stops at the 4th generation: it has no row for any 5th Generation card. The datasheets do not carry power either; grepping all 78 documents for a wattage at any of Cisco's five stated ambients returns nothing outside those two tables. So no document held states this card's draw, and an estimate would be the same number without this sentence.
provenance.relief: RELIEF IS DECLARED, AND WHAT MATTERS ABOUT IT IS THAT IT IS A HANDFUL OF NUMBERS AND NOT A HANDFUL PER PART. This face carries: 11 panel lamps at dome 0.3 (one number, carried by 120 Cisco contracts); 4 ejector brackets, their levers and the grip flanges at out 4.2 (one number, carried by 61 Cisco contracts); 2 captive screw heads at cyl 1.6 (one number, carried by 63 Cisco contracts); 1 asset labels at out 0.2 (one number, carried by 22 Cisco contracts). EVERY MAGNITUDE BELOW IS ESTIMATED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE READING OF WHAT RELIEF IS FOR. The owner's ruling: 'the whole 3d part is kind of interpolated anyway... It's just to give it a realistic view instead of just being a flat 2d... All of the 3d stuff is going to be mostly conjecture unless the vendor provides that data.' So a proudness here is an interpolation for a realistic view, NOT a claim about the hardware, and the confidence token on every feature says so rather than leaving it to be inferred. WHY `estimated` AND NOT `borrowed`, SINCE EVERY NUMBER HERE DOES COME FROM ANOTHER PORTRAYAL PART. `borrowed` is defined as another part's MEASURED figure reused for the same class of hardware, and these origins are not measured - they are the library's first guess at that hardware, and the contracts say so themselves: agr-panel-screw's provenance reads 'estimated - it stands proud but was not measured', agr-psu-dc sources its latch's ARRANGEMENT from a photograph and never its proudness, agr-fan describes its handle and grille by appearance only, and common/led-dot's entire provenance is 'size: estimated'. Spelling that chain `borrowed` would convert a guess into an apparent measurement at one remove, a thousand times over. `source` still names the origin, so the coordinating benefit is kept and only the claim that is not true is dropped. READ THE COUNTS ABOVE AS THEY ARE MEANT: a figure carried by sixty-odd contracts is ONE ESTIMATE WRITTEN SIXTY-ODD TIMES, not sixty-odd readings that happened to agree. One caliper on any one Cisco captive screw, any one ejector lever or any one panel lamp corrects every part in the library that shares it, which is the whole reason the numbers are pooled instead of chosen per card. THE SEARCH FOR A REAL FIGURE WAS RUN FIRST AND IS RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REPEATED: all 112 doc.md extracts for 'protrud', 'extends outward', 'stands proud' and 'clearance in front' - the only vendor in the intake that publishes a projection is UfiSpace, on the S9510-28DC; the per-card dimension tables, including Table A-10 of the older Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide which the current revision dropped, all of which carry H, W, D and weight only; and the ASR 9000 Visio stencil, whose 119 masters are FRONT and REAR elevations with no side, top or isometric view, so it holds no depth axis at all and is closed as a source. Figure 48 of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide and Figure 1-8 of the ISM guide DO show this hardware in three dimensions and are perspective drawings with a vanishing point, so they settle the ARRANGEMENT - bracket off the plate, lever along it, domed screw head proud of both - and nothing about size. STILL REFUSED ON THIS FACE, and these are NOT the same kind of gap: pivot-top - each would need an EIGHTH family number for one or two nodes, which buys a little realism at the cost of another invented figure; left flat deliberately. The ruling sanctions interpolating a PROUDNESS for a realistic view. It does not sanction inventing an APERTURE, which is a dimension a specification is withholding rather than one nobody has measured.
provenance.size: datasheet - Cisco ASR 9900 Series 5th Generation 10-Port 400 Gigabit Ethernet Line Card Data Sheet: 'ASR 9900 4T 5th Generation Service Edge Line Card: 1.68 x 15.87 x 24.00 in.; 28.40 lb (42.67 x 403.10 x 609.60 mm; 12.88 kg)'. Note this is a LONGER card than the 2T and the 4th generation, which are 395.7 - the shell art scales with it.

components.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series 12-Port 100 Gigabit Ethernet Line Card. Twelve QSFP28 ports arranged as six pairs, staggered in two rows - four pairs on one row and two on the other. The 4th-generation shell, but an earlier card than the 16-port and 32-port QSFP28 pair.
components.name: a99-12x100ge

provenance.cages: composed from std/, not drawn. Ganged QSFP pitch measures 18.73 mm off the art against the registry's TE-measured 19.0, so Cisco's shared-wall block is about 1.4 percent tighter; the measured PITCH is carried and the registry's APERTURE is carried, which leaves a nominal 0.23 mm wall. Aperture size is a governed dimension and a drawing is not the place to take it from.
provenance.fan-tray: install guide - 'If the 12-port 100GE line card is inserted in a chassis, it is important to use filler panels that have two screens [A9K-LC-FILR-V2]. This ensures optimal cooling and EMI.' So this card constrains which BLANK its neighbours use, which is a compatibility fact a chassis may want.
provenance.frame: the card is modelled PORTRAIT - x across the card's thickness, y along its width - which is the stencil's own frame and casa's. WHICH WAY A CHASSIS CARRIES IT is the Overview and Reference Guide's 'Chassis Slots' section, quoted because an earlier version of this note had it wrong for three chassis out of seven: 'Cisco ASR 9010 Router: All line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted VERTICALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card. Cisco ASR 9006 Router and Cisco ASR 9904 Router: All chassis line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted HORIZONTALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card. Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' So only the ASR 9006 and the ASR 9904 lay their cards flat and rotate the bay; the other five place this component unrotated. The ejector-lever wording is the tell and it is why the guide is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing - 'top and bottom' means vertical, 'left and right ends' means horizontal, and the RU height of a chassis does not decide it.
provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. CAUTION for anyone re-deriving this: index.json's props.height_in and width_in are the Visio SHAPE box, not the card. They read 1.72 x 14.75 in for EVERY card master, against the datasheet's 1.63 x 15.58 in, and are 5 percent out in both axes. The ART is orthographic and does carry geometry: taking Cisco's stated W - which the spec table says 'includes ejector bracket/lever' - as the full long extent of the art puts the faceplate rectangle at 41.6 mm against a stated H of 41.4, inside half a percent, which is the gate-1 check. So the drawing is the ruler and the shape box is not.
provenance.leds: install guide - 'Each line card has a single tristate Status LED to display card status. Each ... port on the line card has a port status LED visible on the front panel.' The state vocabulary on both is Table 32, 'Port Status and Line Card Status LEDs', of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, transcribed rather than summarised: the card lamp's amber is TWO states, steady during boot and blinking for a software configuration error.
provenance.lifecycle: searched - this part number is not in bulletin EOL15321, which covers the 4th generation Ethernet line card family. No other notice for it is in the intake.
provenance.not-drawn: one thing on the real faceplate is deliberately NOT modelled: the coloured outlines that box each port group. They are real printing - the install guide spells the scheme out for the 400G combo card, 'Ports 0-5 (blue), 10-15 (red), 20-25 (magenta), 30-35 (orange)' - and the stencil draws them per group in solid and dashed strokes. They are omitted because the stencil builds them from many short stroked segments rather than closed rectangles, and guessing at a box that reads as a group boundary would put a line on the drawing that no measurement supports. Port grouping is carried structurally instead, by the port ids and by the lamp clusters that sit at each group's end.
provenance.numbering: THIS MASTER PRINTS NO PORT NUMERALS AS TEXT - all twelve are outlined glyphs, so there is nothing to transcribe and nothing for the numeral matcher every other card here uses. The numbering is therefore taken from the PRINTED POSITION of each glyph, assigned to its nearest bore, and the result is corroborated by the glyph WIDTHS, which is the part that makes it safe rather than merely plausible. The twelve ink boxes all share one cap height of 1.53 mm and differ only in width. On the four-bore column the widths are 0.89, 0.61, 0.92 and 0.92 mm: the one narrow glyph is a figure one, and it falls on the bore that the positional rule numbers 1. On the eight-bore column six glyphs are 0.91-0.99 mm wide and exactly two are double width, 1.89 and 1.68 mm, and those two fall on the bores the rule numbers 10 and 11 - in that order, the wider of the pair being the one containing a zero. So three independent facts agree: position, the single-digit-vs-double-digit split, and which digit is narrow. The card is numbered from 0, and the constant cap height with varying width is also what says these numerals are set ACROSS the card rather than along it, unlike the PID.
provenance.ports: install guide - '12-Port 100-Gigabit Ethernet Line Card with QSFP28 ... provides twelve ports for QSFP28 modules that operate at a rate of 100 Gbps', Figure 19 callout 3. The master draws twelve bores at 4.33 x 15.2 mm, the same QSFP28 bore signature as the 16-port and 32-port cards.
provenance.power: install guide - Table 35 of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, row '12-Port 100-Gigabit Line Card': 1170 W at 27 C, 1150 W at 40 C, 1200 W at 50 C. Note the 40 C figure is LOWER than the 27 C one, which is the only non-monotonic row in that table; max takes the highest of the three regardless, which is what max means. Cisco does not qualify these as typical or maximum.
provenance.relief: RELIEF IS DECLARED, AND WHAT MATTERS ABOUT IT IS THAT IT IS A HANDFUL OF NUMBERS AND NOT A HANDFUL PER PART. This face carries: 13 panel lamps at dome 0.3 (one number, carried by 120 Cisco contracts); 4 ejector brackets, their levers and the grip flanges at out 4.2 (one number, carried by 61 Cisco contracts); 2 captive screw heads at cyl 1.6 (one number, carried by 63 Cisco contracts); 1 asset labels at out 0.2 (one number, carried by 22 Cisco contracts). EVERY MAGNITUDE BELOW IS ESTIMATED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE READING OF WHAT RELIEF IS FOR. The owner's ruling: 'the whole 3d part is kind of interpolated anyway... It's just to give it a realistic view instead of just being a flat 2d... All of the 3d stuff is going to be mostly conjecture unless the vendor provides that data.' So a proudness here is an interpolation for a realistic view, NOT a claim about the hardware, and the confidence token on every feature says so rather than leaving it to be inferred. WHY `estimated` AND NOT `borrowed`, SINCE EVERY NUMBER HERE DOES COME FROM ANOTHER PORTRAYAL PART. `borrowed` is defined as another part's MEASURED figure reused for the same class of hardware, and these origins are not measured - they are the library's first guess at that hardware, and the contracts say so themselves: agr-panel-screw's provenance reads 'estimated - it stands proud but was not measured', agr-psu-dc sources its latch's ARRANGEMENT from a photograph and never its proudness, agr-fan describes its handle and grille by appearance only, and common/led-dot's entire provenance is 'size: estimated'. Spelling that chain `borrowed` would convert a guess into an apparent measurement at one remove, a thousand times over. `source` still names the origin, so the coordinating benefit is kept and only the claim that is not true is dropped. READ THE COUNTS ABOVE AS THEY ARE MEANT: a figure carried by sixty-odd contracts is ONE ESTIMATE WRITTEN SIXTY-ODD TIMES, not sixty-odd readings that happened to agree. One caliper on any one Cisco captive screw, any one ejector lever or any one panel lamp corrects every part in the library that shares it, which is the whole reason the numbers are pooled instead of chosen per card. THE SEARCH FOR A REAL FIGURE WAS RUN FIRST AND IS RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REPEATED: all 112 doc.md extracts for 'protrud', 'extends outward', 'stands proud' and 'clearance in front' - the only vendor in the intake that publishes a projection is UfiSpace, on the S9510-28DC; the per-card dimension tables, including Table A-10 of the older Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide which the current revision dropped, all of which carry H, W, D and weight only; and the ASR 9000 Visio stencil, whose 119 masters are FRONT and REAR elevations with no side, top or isometric view, so it holds no depth axis at all and is closed as a source. Figure 48 of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide and Figure 1-8 of the ISM guide DO show this hardware in three dimensions and are perspective drawings with a vanishing point, so they settle the ARRANGEMENT - bracket off the plate, lever along it, domed screw head proud of both - and nothing about size. STILL REFUSED ON THIS FACE, and these are NOT the same kind of gap: pivot-top - each would need an EIGHTH family number for one or two nodes, which buys a little realism at the cost of another invented figure; left flat deliberately. The ruling sanctions interpolating a PROUDNESS for a realistic view. It does not sanction inventing an APERTURE, which is a dimension a specification is withholding rather than one nobody has measured.
provenance.size: datasheet - Cisco ASR 9000 Series 12-Port 100-Gigabit Ethernet Line Cards Data Sheet: '12-port 100 Gigabit Ethernet line card: 14.5 x 1.63 x 22.02 in.; 28 lb (estimated) (368.3 mm x 41.4 mm x 559.3 mm; 11.7 kg)'. Note the axis order and the missing qualifier: H is the LONG dimension here and the heading is a bare (H x W x D) where the 16-port and 32-port sheets say '(includes ejector bracket/lever)'. Same case as the dual-rate 10GE pair, and handled the same way - the card is modelled at the family's 395.7 because its shell is the SAME DRAWING as the 16-port and 32-port masters, seventeen of seventeen shell features agreeing to 0.00 mm, and one shell cannot be two lengths. 368.3 is the plate; both numbers are recorded. Depth is the sheet's own 559.3, which really is shorter than the 100GE cards that came after it.

provenance.not-drawn: one thing on the real faceplate is deliberately NOT modelled: the coloured outlines that box each port group. provenance.numbering: the master misprints its last port numeral as 32 on a 32-port card numbered from 0. provenance.power: NOT STATED, and this is the record of it. provenance.relief: RELIEF IS DECLARED, AND WHAT MATTERS ABOUT IT IS THAT IT IS A HANDFUL OF NUMBERS AND NOT A HANDFUL PER PART. This face carries: 33 panel lamps at dome 0.3 (one number, carried by 120 Cisco contracts); 4 ejector brackets, their levers and the grip flanges at out 4.2 (one number, carried by 61 Cisco contracts); 2 captive screw heads at cyl 1.6 (one number, carried by 63 Cisco contracts); 1 asset labels at out 0.2 (one number, carried by 22 Cisco contracts). components.description: Cisco A99 400GE Combo Service Edge Line Card, 5th generation. Forty-four ports on one faceplate: twenty-four SFP+ at 10GE, sixteen SFP28 at 10 or 25GE, and four QSFP+/QSFP28 at 40 or 100GE, for 400 Gigabit of aggregate bandwidth. The ports are colour-coded into four groups of eleven and each group carries up to 100GE, so the supported combinations are a table rather than a sum.
components.name: a99-4hg-flex-se

provenance.cages: composed from std/, not drawn. Measured 9.17 x 14.2 mm, which rotated is 14.2 x 9.17 against std/sfp-ganged's SFF-8433 aperture of 14.25 x 10.40: the PITCH dimension agrees to 0.05 mm and the height is 12 percent under, which is the drawn opening sitting inside the bezel cutout. The registry figure is what is placed.
provenance.colour-groups: the guide gives the colour scheme in full - 'Ports 0-5 (blue), 10-15 (red), 20-25 (magenta), 30-35 (orange) support 10GE SFP+ modules; Ports 6-9 (blue), 16-19 (red), 26-29 (magenta), 36-39 (orange) support 10GE/25GE SFP28 modules' - and it is NOT drawn here, for the reason the QSFP cards' group boxes are not: the stencil builds those outlines from many short stroked segments rather than closed rectangles, and a box drawn to look right is a line no measurement supports. provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. index.json's shape box is NOT the card: it reads 1.72 x 14.75 in for every card master against the datasheets' 1.63 x 15.58, five percent out in both axes. The ART is orthographic: taking Cisco's stated W - the spec table says it 'includes ejector bracket/lever' - as the full long extent of the drawing puts the faceplate rectangle at 41.6 mm against a stated H of 41.4, inside half a percent.
provenance.leds: install guide - 'All Ethernet line cards have port Status LEDs on their front panels. Each SFP or XFP port has an adjacent LED to indicate the status of the associated port. That is a gap, and it is different from the QSFP cards, where each port's lamp is drawn separately and IS modelled.
provenance.lifecycle: searched - this part number is not in bulletin EOL15321, which covers the 4th generation Ethernet line card family. No other notice for it is in the intake.
provenance.numbering: the port numerals are transcribed from the master, and the way they were matched to cages is worth recording because two simpler rules each failed on a real card. provenance.lamps: READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING A LAMP POSITION. The nine legends - ACTIVE, FAIL, BOOT, SYNC, CRIT on one line and PWR, SSD, GPS, MAJ/MIN below - are extracted text and their positions are exact. The LAMPS THEMSELVES ARE NOT: they are drawn as small strokes that the extractor cannot separate from the hex vent field around them, so each lamp is placed 3.4 mm left and 1.5 mm above its own legend, which is where the rendered artwork puts them by eye. The names and the count are sourced; the coordinates are a consistent offset, and anyone needing better should re-measure from the master. The state vocabularies are Table 5 of the Overview and Reference Guide where a name matches (FAIL, CRIT, SYNC, SSD and the MAJ/MIN pair); ACTIVE, BOOT, PWR and GPS have no row on that table for this card, so PWR, GPS and ACTIVE take the green/off form their names imply and BOOT carries off/on.
provenance.lifecycle: searched - no end-of-life notice for this part number is in the intake. Cisco's ordering table also lists A99-RP-F-FC, the flexible-consumption variant of the same hardware; it is not modelled separately.
provenance.orientation: modelled LANDSCAPE, as the master draws it and as the card installs - the ASR 9902 is 2RU and the ASR 9903 3RU, and the RPs lie flat.
provenance.ports: datasheet - Cisco ASR 9903 Compact High-Performance Router Data Sheet: 'A set of external interfaces on the front panel includes: console and auxiliary serial ports, two management Ethernet interfaces, a Class A USB port, GPS interface (10Mhz, 1PPS, ToD ports), and two BITS interfaces.' provenance.alarm-out: install guide - 'Each RSP/RP card drives a set of three alarm output contacts. provenance.cages: composed from std/, never drawn. provenance.db9: the ALARM OUT connector is DRAWN, not composed, and it IS declared `class: cutout` - which is a reversal of what these components said until now and the reversal is the point. The earlier version withheld `class: cutout` on the reasoning that a cutout conforming to nothing would corrupt the aperture census L26 keeps. THAT WAS BACKWARDS. L26's own message ends 'if the dimension cannot be sourced yet, this warning is the record of that', and its docstring calls the rule a to-do list for std/ rather than an accusation. CONTRAST cisco/a9k-750w-dc, whose DC terminal block is correctly NOT a cutout: that is hardware bolted to the face rather than a hole punched in it, and the distinction is between a thing that needs an opening and a thing that does not.

components.description: Cisco ASR 9910 and ASR 9906 Route Switch Processor, Service Edge optimised - the card Cisco's guides call the RSP4-S. Four 10-GE SFP+ ports and control of up to seven switch fabrics, two of them on the RSP itself. Ten RJ-45 jacks - two SYNC timing ports configurable as BITS, J.211 or DTI, an IEEE 1588 timestamp port, two inter-chassis sync ports of which ICS1 doubles as the RS232/422 GPS time-of-day input, two management LAN ports, a CMP port, a console and an auxiliary port - plus 10 MHz and 1 PPS SMB clock inputs, a nine-pin alarm output, a USB 2.0 type A port, nine discrete status lamps, a four-character LED dot-matrix display and a LAMP TEST push button.
components.name: a99-rsp-se

provenance.alarm-out: install guide - 'Each RSP/RP card drives a set of three alarm output contacts. Alarm circuitry on the RSP/RP activates dry contact closures that are accessible through the nine-pin Alarm Out connector on the RSP/RP front panel... Both normally-open and normally-closed contacts are available. Only the active RSP/RP drives the alarm outputs.'

Both are drawn on the master as stroked circles with their legends beside them. Worth recording how nearly they were missed: the first extraction pass reported one button, because a circle is a curve and the outline reader skips curves - the second was found by looking at the artwork at 8 px/mm rather than by trusting the count.
provenance.cages: composed from std/, never drawn. The RJ-45s go in as std/rj45-ganged (12.7 x 11.0) rather than std/rj45 (16.0 x 14.0): the IEC 60603-7 single-port cutout is the wrong part for a stacked pair whose ports share walls, and 16.0 will not fit twice across a 41 mm card. The drawn jack measures 10.83 x 12.81, which rotated is 12.81 x 10.83 against the ganged registry's 12.7 x 11.0 - agreement to one percent, which is the check. Timing coax is std/smb, sourced from the same 10-32 UNF figure the registry carries; the USB is std/usb-a.
provenance.db9: the ALARM OUT connector is DRAWN, not composed, and it IS declared `class: cutout` - which is a reversal of what these components said until now and the reversal is the point. There is no std/ part for a D-subminiature DE-9, no `db9` key in spec/schemas/standards.yaml, and no document in this intake dimensions the panel opening; the geometry here is transcribed from the master. The earlier version withheld `class: cutout` on the reasoning that a cutout conforming to nothing would corrupt the aperture census L26 keeps. THAT WAS BACKWARDS. L26's own message ends 'if the dimension cannot be sourced yet, this warning is the record of that', and its docstring calls the rule a to-do list for std/ rather than an accusation. Withholding the declaration did not keep the census clean, it kept a real gap OUT of the one rule built to hold it - a count kept tidy by routing around the detector. So the cutout is declared, the L26 warning stands, and the register is one entry more honest. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a `db9` key in standards.yaml carrying the D-sub panel cutout from MIL-DTL-24308 or its commercial equivalent, plus a std/db9 part. That is a real errand somebody can run, unlike the CFP family's, and nobody has run it. CONTRAST cisco/a9k-750w-dc, whose DC terminal block is correctly NOT a cutout: that is hardware bolted to the face rather than a hole punched in it, and the distinction is between a thing that needs an opening and a thing that does not.

provenance.power: NOT STATED. The ASR 9903 data sheet gives a chassis power envelope and no per-card figure, and the fixed-port Hardware Installation Guide's per-card numbers come from a `show environment` example taken on an ASR 9902, which has no PEC. Table 35 of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide covers the modular-chassis cards only and has no PEC row.
provenance.relief: RELIEF IS DECLARED, AND WHAT MATTERS ABOUT IT IS THAT IT IS A HANDFUL OF NUMBERS AND NOT A HANDFUL PER PART. This face carries: 2 ejector brackets, their levers and the grip flanges at out 4.2 (one number, carried by 61 Cisco contracts); 2 captive screw heads at cyl 1.6 (one number, carried by 63 Cisco contracts); 2 panel lamps at dome 0.3 (one number, carried by 120 Cisco contracts). EVERY MAGNITUDE BELOW IS ESTIMATED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE READING OF WHAT RELIEF IS FOR. The owner's ruling: 'the whole 3d part is kind of interpolated anyway... It's just to give it a realistic view instead of just being a flat 2d... All of the 3d stuff is going to be mostly conjecture unless the vendor provides that data.' So a proudness here is an interpolation for a realistic view, NOT a claim about the hardware, and the confidence token on every feature says so rather than leaving it to be inferred. WHY `estimated` AND NOT `borrowed`, SINCE EVERY NUMBER HERE DOES COME FROM ANOTHER PORTRAYAL PART. `borrowed` is defined as another part's MEASURED figure reused for the same class of hardware, and these origins are not measured - they are the library's first guess at that hardware, and the contracts say so themselves: agr-panel-screw's provenance reads 'estimated - it stands proud but was not measured', agr-psu-dc sources its latch's ARRANGEMENT from a photograph and never its proudness, agr-fan describes its handle and grille by appearance only, and common/led-dot's entire provenance is 'size: estimated'. Spelling that chain `borrowed` would convert a guess into an apparent measurement at one remove, a thousand times over. `source` still names the origin, so the coordinating benefit is kept and only the claim that is not true is dropped. READ THE COUNTS ABOVE AS THEY ARE MEANT: a figure carried by sixty-odd contracts is ONE ESTIMATE WRITTEN SIXTY-ODD TIMES, not sixty-odd readings that happened to agree. One caliper on any one Cisco captive screw, any one ejector lever or any one panel lamp corrects every part in the library that shares it, which is the whole reason the numbers are pooled instead of chosen per card. provenance.size: TWO NUMBERS, and which one this component carries matters. The Cisco ASR 9903 Compact High-Performance Router Data Sheet gives 'Physical dimensions (H x W x D); weight': 1.47 x 16.31 x 15.09 in. The difference is 22.31 mm across and 1.39 mm high, which is an ejector at each end and a rail top and bottom. THE SHAPESHEET FIGURE IS CARRIED, for two reasons. First, a module's `size` in this library is its SLOT ENVELOPE - the bay it occupies - not its faceplate, and the faceplate is what the skin draws. Second, this datasheet's heading is bare '(H x W x D)' where every modular line-card sheet in the intake says '(includes ejector bracket/lever)', and the one other sheet that omits the qualifier - the dual-rate 10GE pair - turned out to be quoting the plate rather than the envelope in exactly the same way. So 414.27 x 37.34 is recorded here as the plate and is what the drawing shows; 436.58 x 38.73 is the envelope and is what a bay is sized from. Both axes of the carried figure come from one source, which is the rule a power module 3.66 mm too wide taught tonight.
provenance.slices: install guide - 'The ports are grouped in slice 4 and slice 5. These slices are marked in blue and purple' and 'A slice is a logical grouping of physical ports.' components.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series 16-Port 100 Gigabit Ethernet Service Edge Line Card, 4th generation. Sixteen QSFP28/QSFP+ ports at 100 Gigabit Ethernet, on the same faceplate as the A9K-16X100GE-TR. provenance.cages: composed from std/, not drawn. Aperture size is a governed dimension and a drawing is not the place to take it from.
provenance.frame: the card is modelled PORTRAIT - x across the card's thickness, y along its width - which is the stencil's own frame and casa's. provenance.se-tr: the -SE and -TR masters of this card are the SAME DRAWING: extracted port centres agree to 0.00 mm across every port, which is what one expects of two part numbers that differ in buffering and table scale rather than in sheet metal. provenance.size: INFERRED, and here is the whole of the inference. The -SE and -TR masters are the same drawing - extracted port centres agree to 0.00 mm at all sixteen ports - and the -TR's 41.4 x 395.7 x 604.5 mm is a datasheet fact. Two part numbers drawn on one faceplate share that faceplate's size. This is not the 'scale one card from its neighbour' move the intake warns against: that warning is about the -X- generation, whose master genuinely differs from the non-X one by 5.64 mm, and the same check is what shows these two do not differ at all. Weight is NOT inferred and is absent - the two variants differ in buffer memory, which has mass.
provenance.sources: READ THIS FIRST. This is one of three part numbers that have artwork in Cisco's own Visio stencil and NO specification anywhere in the 78-document intake. It is real - the Secure Boot Product List prints 'ASR 9000 16-port 100GE QSFP SE line card' against it, IOS XR 7.10.2, 24.2.1 and 24.3.2 firmware tables carry it, and bulletin EOL15321 gives it an end-of-sale date and a replacement. What does not exist is a data sheet: no port arrangement, no LED table, no power draw, no dimensions, and no entry on Cisco's own scraped datasheet-listing index. So GEOMETRY here is stencil-derived and the card carries no invented figure.

provenance.cages: composed from std/, not drawn. provenance.frame: the card is modelled PORTRAIT - x across the card's thickness, y along its width - which is the stencil's own frame and casa's. WHICH WAY A CHASSIS CARRIES IT is the Overview and Reference Guide's 'Chassis Slots' section, quoted because an earlier version of this note had it wrong for three chassis out of seven: 'Cisco ASR 9010 Router: All line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted VERTICALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card. Cisco ASR 9006 Router and Cisco ASR 9904 Router: All chassis line cards and RSP cards are front- facing and mounted HORIZONTALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card. Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. index.json's shape box is NOT the card: it reads 1.72 x 14.75 in for every card master against the datasheets' 1.63 x 15.58, five percent out in both axes. provenance.numbering: the port numerals are transcribed from the master, and the way they were matched to cages is worth recording because two simpler rules each failed on a real card. components.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series 2-Port 100 Gigabit Ethernet DX Line Card with CFP. Two very large CFP cages - 75.68 mm long, the biggest aperture on any card in this library - each with four jackscrews at its corners and an A/L lamp beneath it. An original- generation card at 43.7 mm thick, not a 4th-generation one.
components.name: a9k-2x100ge-se

provenance.aperture: DRAWN, NOT COMPOSED, AND DECLARED `class: cutout` ANYWAY - which takes an L26 warning, and the warning is the point. THE CFP MSA HARDWARE SPECIFICATION DOES NOT CARRY A BEZEL OPENING, and that is by design rather than by omission. Revision 1.4 of 7 June 2010 was fetched and read in full: section 5.3 says 'The detailed CFP module dimensions are located in a separate document hosted on the CFP MSA Website', and it says the same thing again for the railing system and again for the electrical connector. Its only mechanical table, Table 5-1, is weight, flatness and roughness. The separate document is members-only. The cages here are transcribed from the master at 11.51 x 75.68 mm and conform to nothing, because there is nothing to conform to. The earlier instinct on cards like this was to withhold `class: cutout` so the aperture census stayed clean; that is backwards. L26's own message ends 'if the dimension cannot be sourced yet, this warning is the record of that'. A census kept tidy by not declaring a cutout has been routed around, not satisfied. WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, stated so a contributor is not sent on an errand that cannot be run: CFP MSA membership and the baseline drawing it gives access to, or a Cisco mechanical drawing of this faceplate. NOT 'look harder' - this is not a search that failed, it is a specification that withholds the figure. Contrast the XFP on the 4-port and 2-port 10GE MPAs in this library, where INF-8077i gives the bezel opening outright in two figures and the only thing missing had been anyone looking outside the vendor's own guide.
provenance.lamps: drawing - the master prints 'A/L0' and 'A/L1' as text and draws the indicator itself as a small triangle rather than a rectangle or a circle, which is why the lamp-shape detectors used elsewhere in this library find nothing on it. The lamp is placed at its legend. NO PER-CARD LED TABLE EXISTS, so the three A/L states are the family's shape and are a BORROWING, flagged as one. The eight 2.88 mm circles at the cage corners are JACKSCREWS, not lamps - a CFP module is retained by four of them - and are not modelled as indicators.

components.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series 4-Port 100 Gigabit Ethernet LAN Line Card. Four QSFP28 ports in two pairs, each pair with an A/L lamp at either end. Cisco calls this one a low-power design and it is the QSFP28 4-port card, NOT the CPAK A9K-4X100GE-SE and -TR which share the number and are a different card - see `identity`. Breaks out to sixteen 10GE.
components.name: a9k-4x100ge

provenance.cages: drawing, HANDED TO THE BUILDER RATHER THAN DETECTED, and the reason is worth recording. Every other QSFP card in this stencil paints an open bore at #0c0c0c and the cage detector keys on that darkness. This master draws POPULATED cages instead - the housing at #595959 with its gold contact fingers showing - so there is no dark bore anywhere on it and the detector returns nothing. The four cages are measured off the master at 7.57, 105.67 / 125.08 / 204.81 / 224.22, each 8.45 x 19.16 mm, and passed in explicitly. The scale is corroborated the usual way: at the 41.4 anchor those cages are within 4.4 percent of the A99-12X100GE's, and at 43.7 they would be 10 percent out.
provenance.chassis: datasheet - c78-740092, Table 2: 'Chassis compatibility: Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis'. All seven, stated outright, which is rarer in this family than it should be.
provenance.frame: the card is modelled PORTRAIT - x across the card's thickness, y along its width - which is the stencil's own frame and casa's. WHICH WAY A CHASSIS CARRIES IT is the Overview and Reference Guide's 'Chassis Slots' section, quoted because an earlier version of this note had it wrong for three chassis out of seven: 'Cisco ASR 9010 Router: All line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted VERTICALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card. Cisco ASR 9006 Router and Cisco ASR 9904 Router: All chassis line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted HORIZONTALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card. Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' So only the ASR 9006 and the ASR 9904 lay their cards flat and rotate the bay; the other five place this component unrotated. The ejector-lever wording is the tell and it is why the guide is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing - 'top and bottom' means vertical, 'left and right ends' means horizontal, and the RU height of a chassis does not decide it.
provenance.identity: TWO DIFFERENT CARDS SHARE THIS PART NUMBER'S ROOT and getting them mixed up would put a CPAK aperture on a QSFP28 card. Cisco's own data sheets separate them: c78-733790, 'Cisco ASR 9000 Series 4-Port and 8-Port 100 Gigabit Ethernet Line Cards', is CPAK throughout and covers A9K-4X100GE-SE and A9K-4X100GE-TR at 28 lb; c78-740092 is titled 'Cisco ASR 9000 4-port 100GE LAN line card A9K-4X100GE', mentions QSFP28 and no CPAK at all, and gives 19.7 lb. provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. provenance.aperture: DRAWN, NOT COMPOSED, AND DECLARED `class: cutout` ANYWAY - which takes an L26 warning, and the warning is the point. CPAK IS CISCO-PROPRIETARY AND HAS NO MSA AT ALL. There is no multi-source agreement, no public mechanical specification and no bezel-opening figure anywhere in the 78-document intake. The cages here are transcribed from the master at 13.92 x 37.01 mm and conform to nothing, because there is nothing to conform to. The earlier instinct on cards like this was to withhold `class: cutout` so the aperture census stayed clean; that is backwards. L26's own message ends 'if the dimension cannot be sourced yet, this warning is the record of that'. A census kept tidy by not declaring a cutout has been routed around, not satisfied. WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS, stated so a contributor is not sent on an errand that cannot be run: CFP MSA membership and the baseline drawing it gives access to, or a Cisco mechanical drawing of this faceplate. NOT 'look harder' - this is not a search that failed, it is a specification that withholds the figure. Contrast the XFP on the 4-port and 2-port 10GE MPAs in this library, where INF-8077i gives the bezel opening outright in two figures and the only thing missing had been anyone looking outside the vendor's own guide.

WHICH WAY A CHASSIS CARRIES IT is the Overview and Reference Guide's 'Chassis Slots' section, quoted because an earlier version of this note had it wrong for three chassis out of seven: 'Cisco ASR 9010 Router: All line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted VERTICALLY, with ejector levers and captive screws at the top and bottom of each card. Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' Cisco ASR 9906 Router: ... mounted vertically ... Cisco ASR 9910 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9922 Router: ... vertically ... Cisco ASR 9912 Router: ... vertically.' So only the ASR 9006 and the ASR 9904 lay their cards flat and rotate the bay; the other five place this component unrotated. The ejector-lever wording is the tell and it is why the guide is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing - 'top and bottom' means vertical, 'left and right ends' means horizontal, and the RU height of a chassis does not decide it.
provenance.layout: drawing - the Cisco Visio master, scaled to the datasheet's own overall dimensions. CAUTION for anyone re-deriving this: index.json's props.height_in and width_in are the Visio SHAPE box, not the card. They read 1.72 x 14.75 in for EVERY card master, against the datasheet's 1.63 x 15.58 in, and are 5 percent out in both axes. The ART is orthographic and does carry geometry: taking Cisco's stated W - which the spec table says 'includes ejector bracket/lever' - as the full long extent of the art puts the faceplate rectangle at 41.6 mm against a stated H of 41.4, inside half a percent, which is the gate-1 check. So the drawing is the ruler and the shape box is not.
provenance.leds: install guide - 'Each line card has a single tristate Status LED to display card status. Each ... port on the line card has a port status LED visible on the front panel.' The state vocabulary on both is Table 32, 'Port Status and Line Card Status LEDs', of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, transcribed rather than summarised: the card lamp's amber is TWO states, steady during boot and blinking for a software configuration error.
provenance.lifecycle: searched - no end-of-life notice for this part number is in the intake, and it is not named in bulletin EOL15321.
provenance.not-drawn: one thing on the real faceplate is deliberately NOT modelled: the coloured outlines that box each port group. They are real printing - the install guide spells the scheme out for the 400G combo card, 'Ports 0-5 (blue), 10-15 (red), 20-25 (magenta), 30-35 (orange)' - and the stencil draws them per group in solid and dashed strokes. They are omitted because the stencil builds them from many short stroked segments rather than closed rectangles, and guessing at a box that reads as a group boundary would put a line on the drawing that no measurement supports. provenance.ports: install guide - '8-Port 100-Gigabit Ethernet Line Card with QSFP28/QSFPDD': 'Six QSFP28 ports' and 'Two QSFP-DD ports', with Figure 22 callout 2 'Two 400GE QSFP-DD connectors'. provenance.power: NOT STATED, and this is the record of it. provenance.relief: RELIEF IS DECLARED, AND WHAT MATTERS ABOUT IT IS THAT IT IS A HANDFUL OF NUMBERS AND NOT A HANDFUL PER PART. This face carries: 9 panel lamps at dome 0.3 (one number, carried by 120 Cisco contracts); 4 ejector brackets, their levers and the grip flanges at out 4.2 (one number, carried by 61 Cisco contracts); 2 captive screw heads at cyl 1.6 (one number, carried by 63 Cisco contracts); 1 asset labels at out 0.2 (one number, carried by 22 Cisco contracts). EVERY MAGNITUDE BELOW IS ESTIMATED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE READING OF WHAT RELIEF IS FOR. The owner's ruling: 'the whole 3d part is kind of interpolated anyway... It's just to give it a realistic view instead of just being a flat 2d... All of the 3d stuff is going to be mostly conjecture unless the vendor provides that data.' So a proudness here is an interpolation for a realistic view, NOT a claim about the hardware, and the confidence token on every feature says so rather than leaving it to be inferred. WHY `estimated` AND NOT `borrowed`, SINCE EVERY NUMBER HERE DOES COME FROM ANOTHER PORTRAYAL PART. `borrowed` is defined as another part's MEASURED figure reused for the same class of hardware, and these origins are not measured - they are the library's first guess at that hardware, and the contracts say so themselves: agr-panel-screw's provenance reads 'estimated - it stands proud but was not measured', agr-psu-dc sources its latch's ARRANGEMENT from a photograph and never its proudness, agr-fan describes its handle and grille by appearance only, and common/led-dot's entire provenance is 'size: estimated'. Spelling that chain `borrowed` would convert a guess into an apparent measurement at one remove, a thousand times over. `source` still names the origin, so the coordinating benefit is kept and only the claim that is not true is dropped. READ THE COUNTS ABOVE AS THEY ARE MEANT: a figure carried by sixty-odd contracts is ONE ESTIMATE WRITTEN SIXTY-ODD TIMES, not sixty-odd readings that happened to agree. One caliper on any one Cisco captive screw, any one ejector lever or any one panel lamp corrects every part in the library that shares it, which is the whole reason the numbers are pooled instead of chosen per card. THE SEARCH FOR A REAL FIGURE WAS RUN FIRST AND IS RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REPEATED: all 112 doc.md extracts for 'protrud', 'extends outward', 'stands proud' and 'clearance in front' - the only vendor in the intake that publishes a projection is UfiSpace, on the S9510-28DC; the per-card dimension tables, including Table A-10 of the older Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide which the current revision dropped, all of which carry H, W, D and weight only; and the ASR 9000 Visio stencil, whose 119 masters are FRONT and REAR elevations with no side, top or isometric view, so it holds no depth axis at all and is closed as a source. Figure 48 of the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide and Figure 1-8 of the ISM guide DO show this hardware in three dimensions and are perspective drawings with a vanishing point, so they settle the ARRANGEMENT - bracket off the plate, lever along it, domed screw head proud of both - and nothing about size. STILL REFUSED ON THIS FACE, and these are NOT the same kind of gap: pivot-top - each would need an EIGHTH family number for one or two nodes, which buys a little realism at the cost of another invented figure; left flat deliberately. The ruling sanctions interpolating a PROUDNESS for a realistic view. It does not sanction inventing an APERTURE, which is a dimension a specification is withholding rather than one nobody has measured.

components.name: a9k-8x100g-lb-se

provenance.aperture: DRAWN, NOT COMPOSED, AND DECLARED `class: cutout` ANYWAY - which takes an L26 warning, and the warning is the point. CPAK IS CISCO-PROPRIETARY AND HAS NO MSA AT ALL. There is no multi-source agreement, no public mechanical specification and no bezel-opening figure anywhere in the 78-document intake. The cages here are transcribed from the master at 13.92 x 37.01 mm and conform to nothing, because there is nothing to conform to. The earlier instinct on cards like this was to withhold `class: cutout` so the aperture census stayed clean; that is backwards. L26's own message ends 'if the dimension cannot be sourced yet, this warning is the record of that'. A census kept tidy by not declaring a cutout has been routed around, not satisfied.
